claims.text: Enhanced configurational entropy is the primary factor governing the high-temperature structural stability of high-entropy nanoalloys.
Enhanced configurational entropy is the primary factor governing the high-temperature chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys.
Enhanced configurational entropy retards atomic diffusion.
Enhanced configurational entropy inhibits elemental segregation.
A minor dopant that favors local ordering can reduce the alloy's configurational entropy.
Inducing subtle composition gradients can produce an entropy-reduced comparison variant.
An inert atmosphere avoids oxidation during high-temperature treatment.
Annealing for 24 hours at approximately 700–900°C allows diffusion processes to occur.
High configurational entropy promotes a homogeneous atomic distribution.
Slower atomic diffusion reduces phase segregation.
Slower atomic diffusion reduces grain coarsening.
Reducing configurational entropy leads to faster atomic diffusion.
Reducing configurational entropy leads to localized elemental clustering.
Reducing configurational entropy promotes secondary-phase formation.
After the specified heat treatment, the standard high-entropy nanoparticles will retain a fine, homogeneous, single-phase structure with minimal segregation.
Relative to the standard alloy, the entropy-reduced variant will exhibit greater grain coarsening, phase separation, or elemental segregation.
Uniformly synthesized high-entropy nanoalloys are known to retain homogeneous single-phase structures during high-temperature stability tests.
The prediction applies when mixing entropy is sufficiently large relative to segregation forces.
Dominant local chemical interactions or impurity effects can cause deviation from the proposed entropy-controlled mechanism.
